meeting_header:
Date: 2028-07-28 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Claire Wong (Redwood SE), Marta Alvarez (Aquila, Head of ML), Devon Barker (Aquila, CTO), Priya Nair (Aquila, SRE Lead)
summary: Discovery focused on reliability/incident tolerance: Aquila needs multi-region fallbacks, clear SLA tiers, and a pilot to validate Redwood Dedicated latency under peak traffic. Security/KMS and private VPC discussed as gating items for Private deployment evaluation.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — Samir from Redwood, Claire my SE. Could you each do a quick intro?
[00:12] Marta: Marta Alvarez, head of ML at Aquila. We run inference for clinical triage and internal summarization, latency sensitive.
[00:22] Devon: Devon here, CTO. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for compliance and uptime.
[00:30] Priya: Priya, SRE. I'm mostly here for incident tolerance and routing questions.
[00:36] Samir: Great. High level goal today is to understand your reliability needs and what would make you comfortable running production on Redwood — whether Hosted, Dedicated or Private.
[00:48] Claire: Quick note, we'll talk about fallbacks, multi-region routing, and SLA tiers. Also Claire will go through some of the architecture options.
[00:56] Marta: We're aiming for 99.95% for user-facing features and 99.99% for internal billing workflows — that's our desired SLO split, roughly.
[01:10] Devon: And if you can do that across regions — we operate in NA and EU and want failover with under 1 second added latency ideally.
[01:22] Claire: Ok. Two parts: how Redwood routes and fallback, and whether we recommend Hosted with global endpoints or Dedicated pools with multi-region replication.
[01:34] Samir: Quick question, are you planning to keep PII in requests? That determines Private/VPC discussions.
[01:40] Marta: Some do contain PHI-ish data, so we need KMS and audit logs — likely at least a Private control plane or Dedicated with strict retention.
[01:50] Priya: SOC2 and ISO27001 checks are a must. Also we need key rotation and HSM integration for production.
[02:02] Claire: Understood. For Hosted, we offer SOC2 attested endpoints and bring-your-own-KMS for certain tiers, but Private gives you the most control over KMS/HSM and VPC.
[02:18] Samir: Now on routing: Redwood supports policy-based routing by latency/region/customer tier. Our standard fallback is to route to a compatible model variant in a secondary region if the primary pool is unhealthy.
[02:34] Priya: How do you define unhealthy? Node failures or whole region?
[02:38] Claire: Health is a mix — per-instance heartbeat, queue depth, and tail latency thresholds. If we detect sustained degradation or full pool outage we route according to configured policy — e.g., failover to warm standby in another region or to a cheaper model variant in same region.
[02:54] Marta: What's the expected added latency on a cross-region fallback?
[02:58] Claire: Typically cross-region adds network RTT plus model execution time — in practice we've seen 80–200ms extra for NA<>EU depending on model size and KV cache locality. For heavy stateful KV cache use cases, cold cache fallbacks can be larger.
[03:15] Devon: That 200ms could be a problem for our triage flow on mobile. Can we keep prefix cache in sync across regions?
[03:23] Claire: We have prefix/KV caching strategies — you can configure synchronous replication for small state or accept eventual consistency. Synchronous adds overhead, we usually recommend async replication with short TTLs and sticky routing for lowest latency.
[03:37] Priya: Do you support sticky sessions + weighted routing?
[03:41] Samir: Yes, sticky routing by user or conversation id is supported, and weighted policies let you send X% to standby for canary.
[03:48] Marta: Ok. About SLA — do you offer financially backed SLAs for Dedicated?
[03:54] Claire: Dedicated comes with an SLA (99.95% by default) and options to increase with committed capacity. Hosted has best-effort for lower tiers and SLA for enterprise plans. Private is contractual/enterprise.
[04:06] Devon: What about fallback to different model families? If high-capacity model is unavailable, can you route to a smaller but compatible model? We care about graceful degradation.
[04:15] Claire: Yes, that's standard. We maintain model variants and compatible tokenizer/response shaping so you can fallback to smaller quantized variants. We also support automated quality gating — if the quality drop exceeds threshold we'll route to the configured policy like queue or degrade less-sensitive features.
[04:32] Marta: Any chance of hallucination spikes during fallback? We need to understand risk for clinical use.
[04:38] Claire: That's why we pair fallback with eval hooks — you can run smoke checks on a subset of requests to measure regression and have automatic rollback or alerts.
[04:47] Priya: How quick is failback to primary region once restored?
[04:51] Samir: Failback can be automatic based on health checks or manual. We default to gradual shifting back (weighted rollback) to avoid slamming primary pools — usually over a few minutes.
[05:02] Devon: For Dedicated, if a whole AZ goes down, do you replicate capacity across AZs automatically?
[05:08] Claire: Dedicated pools are typically deployed across AZs in a region; cross-region is an explicit config. We can set minimum healthy instances and autoscale to keep capacity, but cross-region failover requires provisioning warm standby or reserve capacity in target region.
[05:24] Marta: Cost question — how much extra for warm standby across regions?
[05:27] Samir: Warm standby is billed as reserved capacity at a partial rate — we can send a pricing sheet. It depends on GPU types and model footprints; Claire will follow up with estimates.
[05:37] Priya: From an SRE perspective, we also need tracing hooks and per-request IDs for audit.
[05:43] Claire: Yep, we emit trace spans and have per-route logging; you can integrate with your observability. For Private we can push logs to your SIEM, or for Hosted we provide secure log delivery and retention controls.
[05:58] Devon: About canaries — we want to gradually roll new model versions without impacting latency SLOs. How does Redwood handle traffic split for canaries?
[06:06] Samir: Canary is first-class: route X% to new version, monitor latency/quality, automatic rollback on threshold. You can also do shadowing.
[06:15] Marta: For our pilot, we'd like a 2-week POC on Dedicated with a small committed pool in NA and warm standby in EU. Can you support benchmarks with our prompt set?
[06:24] Claire: Absolutely. We'll run a benchmark using your prompts and traffic profile; we'll instrument tail-latency and 95/99 percentiles.
[06:31] Priya: We'll need a test harness that can replay traffic and a script to simulate AZ outage.
[06:36] Claire: We can provide a load test harness and run injected-failure tests in a controlled window.
[06:41] Samir: I'll attach the benchmark plan and Claire will lead the tech session.
[06:46] Devon: If we go Private later, what's the lift? Network and HSM integration is our main concern.
[06:51] Claire: Private involves a control-plane handshake, VPN/VPC peering or direct connect, and deployment of the runtime in your environment (or our customer-dedicated VPC). HSM/KMS integration requires some ops work but we have guides and an onboarding team. Typical lead time 8–12 weeks for on-prem, shorter for VPC.
[07:10] Marta: For compliance we need audit logs retention 7 years for some flows; can Redwood handle long-term retention?
[07:16] Samir: Yes, audit logs can be exported to your object store; retention policies are configurable as an add-on.
[07:22] Priya: In the event of a region-level incident, are there automatic fallbacks for in-flight requests or do those fail?
[07:28] Claire: In-flight is tricky — some requests may fail if state is lost, but for stateless generation we re-route new requests. We can mitigate by keeping short request retries and idempotency keys, and by employing sticky routing so most active conversations stay in one healthy pool.
[07:45] Marta: Ok. Can you walk through a hypothetical incident scenario? Say EU region suffers networking partition, and primary pool goes to 0.
[07:53] Claire: We detect via healthchecks, then the routing plane increments weight to standby region, spin up any reserve capacity if configured, and begin routing new requests. If you have synchronous replication for KV, we may fall back slower but with less state loss; otherwise, expect cold-starts on cache and some latency spike.
[08:11] Devon: For cold-starts, how much time to warm a model on a GPU?
[08:15] Claire: Depends model size and quantization. A medium LLM on latest GPUs can warm in 8–30 seconds if image cached; larger models longer. That's why we recommend warm pool for critical services.
[08:25] Samir: We'll propose a pilot config: small Dedicated pool in NA with 20% warm reserve in EU and routing policies that failover to a quantized smaller variant if warm reserve is exhausted.
[08:36] Marta: Sounds reasonable. For the smaller variant, will outputs be formatted the same? Our downstream parsers rely on structure.
[08:42] Claire: We provide structured output shaping and function-calling wrappers so format stays consistent; if you fall back to a variant we'll try to map outputs but quality/regression checks are advised.
[08:55] Priya: We need to confirm RPO/RTO expectations in the contract.
[08:59] Samir: We'll include those in the SLA sheet. Typically RTO for Dedicated with warm standby is minutes; RPO depends on replication config.
[09:08] Marta: For the pilot, our metrics of success: tail latency P95 < 350ms, P99 < 600ms during normal, and degradation during failover limited to < 1s additional latency. Also zero unintentional data exfiltration and SOC2 pass.
[09:26] Claire: Noted. We'll design the benchmark and run a few failure injection tests to validate.
[09:32] Samir: Any legal/procurement blockers?
[09:35] Devon: We have a mandatory DPA review and need to confirm data residency clauses.
[09:39] Samir: We'll send security and compliance pack.
[09:42] Marta: One more: do you offer per-route rate limits and circuit breakers?
[09:46] Claire: Yes, per-route quotas, circuit breakers, and backpressure strategies. You can configure drop policies vs queueing.
[09:54] Priya: On monitoring, do you provide token-level cost breakdowns? We want to map spend to teams.
[09:59] Samir: Yes, console shows token, request-level cost and latency breakdown by route and key.
[10:05] Devon: For the benchmark we need exportable CSVs.
[10:08] Claire: Exportable metrics and traces are included.
[10:12] Marta: Ok, next steps recap?
[10:15] Samir: I'll send Dedicated vs Hosted pricing and warm-standby estimates, Claire will schedule the 90-min technical deep dive and benchmark run, Marta will send prompts and traffic profile by Friday.
[10:25] Devon: Sound good. Anything else?
[10:28] Priya: One ask — include runbook templates for failover and rollback.
[10:31] Claire: We'll include runbook samples.
[10:34] Samir: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs.
[10:37] Marta: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:39] [call ends]
